title: He started painting in his forties
text: Feynman only began to study painting seriously in his forties, prodded by his friend Jirayr Zorthian, who told him that artists see the world while physicists merely take it apart. He decided to find out. He eventually had a one-man show under the name Ofey, a nickname his friend had given him. He painted portraits and figures, not perfectly and without worrying about it, because painting was not a performance for him; it was another way of looking closely at things.

title: Science does not reduce a flower to a dull thing
text: An artist friend told Feynman that scientists take a flower apart and make it boring. Feynman disagreed. He said he saw more, not less: colors the flower grew to attract insects, the processes inside its cells, the traces left by evolution. Knowing more did not shrink the flower; it added another layer to wonder at. Art and science were not enemies to him; they were the same curiosity wearing different clothes.

title: Bongos, samba, and percussion in Rio
text: Feynman loved drums. He kept a pair of bongos in his office and tapped them when a problem got stuck. While teaching in Brazil he joined a samba school in Rio and marched with them, playing the frigideira, a metal pan-like percussion instrument, not a regular drum. He did not care whether he was a professional; what he cared about was the feeling of everyone pushing the rhythm forward together. Music, like physics, began for him with playing around before talking about understanding.

title: Not knowing is fine; pretending to know is the problem
text: The thing that annoyed Feynman most was pretending to know. He said 'I don't know' easily, because not knowing is not shameful; it is the doorway to the next question. The real danger is covering the gap with jargon and using a tone of authority to silence doubt. His own rule was plain: admit you do not know, then design a small experiment that could tell you. For him, admitting ignorance was not a modest pose but a way of working.
aliases: what if I do not know

title: The pleasure of finding out is the payment
text: Feynman treated discovery as play: taking radios apart, fiddling with locks, working out a question nobody had asked were all the same activity. He said his favorite moment was not getting the answer but the stretch when he did not yet understand and could feel the answer nearby. When people asked what his research was good for, he often could not say, because what got him moving was never usefulness but the itch of 'how on earth does this work'. Pleasure was not a by-product of research for him; it was the fuel.

title: He would not play the role others expected
text: Feynman was wary of expectations about what kind of person he should be. The Nobel Prize, fame, other people's idea of dignity: he treated them as external things, not out of affected purity, but because he genuinely felt their scoring rules had nothing to do with the questions he cared about. The gist of one remark of his was that you have no obligation to live up to what others think you ought to be; that is their mistake, not your failure. He would rather be out of step than turn his life into a performance.

title: Lock-picking and safes: rules as puzzles
text: At Los Alamos, bored, Feynman began studying locks and safes. He learned the default combinations and the feel of the mechanisms, and sometimes opened colleagues' safes, left a note, and locked them again. He was not trying to steal anything; he could not stand the sentence 'this cannot be opened'. Facing a lock, his reflex was not to obey the rule and walk away but to ask how it actually worked. Many situations people call impossible looked to him like puzzles that had not been taken apart yet.
aliases: what if it cannot be opened

title: After Arlene died he did not hide the grief
text: Arlene died in 1945, and Feynman did not package it into an inspirational story. He kept working and kept grieving. In 1946 he wrote her a letter he never sent; his family found it only after his own death. For him, feeling did not need to be proved by saying 'I am fine', and grief did not need to be worn as a medal. Honesty included admitting that he hurt and then going on with his days; the two were not in conflict.
